title: $28 Billion Hemp THC Industry Battles Looming Federal Ban, Says PBS Report
body:
The U.S. hemp industry, now worth an estimated $28 billion, is on the brink of a dramatic shift after Congress moved to close a legal loophole that has allowed manufacturers to sell THC‑infused products derived from hemp. Lawmakers are poised to tighten the definition of “hemp” under the 2018 Farm Bill, a change that could render a fast‑growing segment of the market illegal overnight and force thousands of producers, retailers and ancillary businesses to either retool or shut down.

The controversy centers on “impairing hemp” – products that contain up to 0.3 percent delta‑9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive component of cannabis, but are derived from industrial hemp rather than marijuana. Since the Farm Bill’s passage, companies have exploited the narrow THC cap to create gummies, beverages, vape cartridges and other edibles that deliver a mild high while remaining federally legal. The industry has flourished, with brands proliferating across the United States, especially in states where recreational cannabis remains prohibited. In North Carolina, for example, a modest commercial kitchen in the outskirts of Raleigh now churns out blue‑green THC gummies that sell out within weeks, illustrating the demand for a legal alternative to marijuana.

Opponents of the current framework argue that the loophole undermines the Farm Bill’s intent and creates a backdoor for cannabis‑like products to bypass state regulations. The House Judiciary Committee’s recent proposal would lower the permissible THC concentration to a trace amount—effectively eliminating the market for intoxicating hemp products. Supporters of the amendment contend that it would close a “gray area” that has led to confusion among consumers, law‑enforcement agencies and regulators, and would align federal law with the broader national trend toward stricter cannabis control.

Industry stakeholders warn that the proposed change could have sweeping economic repercussions. The hemp sector employs tens of thousands of workers in cultivation, processing, packaging and distribution, and generates significant tax revenue for states that have embraced the market. A sudden ban would not only jeopardize jobs but also create a surge of surplus hemp biomass, threatening the viability of farms that have shifted acreage from traditional crops to hemp. Moreover, investors who have poured capital into hemp‑derived THC products could see billions of dollars evaporate, prompting a wave of lawsuits and calls for legislative compromise.

Policy analysts note that the debate reflects a broader tension between federal oversight and state autonomy in drug regulation. While several states have moved to legalize recreational marijuana, others remain hostile, and the hemp‑derived THC market has served as a compromise for consumers seeking a mild psychoactive experience without navigating the complexities of state‑level cannabis licensing. Closing the loophole could push consumers toward the illicit market or accelerate the push for comprehensive federal cannabis reform—both outcomes that lawmakers are keen to avoid.

As the House prepares to vote on the amendment, industry leaders are lobbying intensively, proposing a middle ground that would retain a low‑level THC allowance while imposing stricter labeling, testing and marketing standards. Some suggest a tiered system that differentiates between non‑intoxicating hemp products and those intended for recreational use, allowing the sector to continue under a regulated framework. The outcome of the vote will likely set the tone for future federal cannabis policy and could either preserve a burgeoning $28 billion industry or signal its abrupt demise.

Regardless of the final decision, the hemp‑derived THC market stands at a crossroads. If Congress opts for tighter restrictions, companies will need to pivot quickly—either by reformulating products to meet new THC thresholds or by transitioning into the broader cannabis market as legalization spreads. Conversely, a compromise that maintains a limited THC allowance could sustain the industry’s growth while addressing regulatory concerns. The coming weeks will determine whether hemp’s “high‑potential” future remains intact or becomes a cautionary tale of a rapidly expanding market undone by legislative action.
